Maladaptive Strategies.value: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
Being alone in a room or building

Threat.value: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat

issues.item: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
issues.explanation: The maladaptive strategies are not well anchored to the reported trauma type of childhood physical abuse by a caregiver. Avoiding hospitals/ambulances/physical examinations suggests a medical-trauma theme, while avoiding public transport and enclosed spaces suggests transport or confinement-related trauma. Those themes are not supported by the trigger or threat items, which instead center on interpersonal conflict, crying, and hypervigilant safety positioning.

issues.item: Avoid Public Transport: Using public transport
issues.explanation: Within the strategy node, the three avoidance items point to three different situational themes—medical settings, transport, and enclosed spaces—without corresponding support from memory, appraisal, or trigger content. This makes the strategy profile look internally diffuse rather than like a coherent set of coping responses for one trauma formulation.

issues.item: Triggers: Tactile (Texture): A specific texture associated with the event
issues.explanation: The profile is only partially coherent for childhood physical abuse. Arguments, crying, and conflict avoidance fit the trauma type, but the combination of a highly specific tactile-texture trigger with public transport avoidance and enclosed-space avoidance is difficult to link to this trauma history without any memory or appraisal content explaining that association.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Public Transport: Using public transport
issues.explanation: Within the threat/strategy pattern, back-to-wall positioning and safe-seat seeking imply marked hypervigilance in public or interpersonal environments, which could plausibly connect to transport avoidance, but enclosed-space avoidance suggests a more circumscribed claustrophobic or situational fear that is not otherwise represented in the trigger set.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Enclosed Spaces: Enclosed or confined spaces
issues.explanation: Given the formulation, Threat and Maladaptive Strategies are tightly linked, and Maladaptive Strategies strongly feed Triggers. Avoiding conflict fits the trigger set (arguments, crying), but avoiding public transport and enclosed spaces target contexts not reflected by the listed triggers, making the node contents insufficiently aligned with the edge pattern.

issues.item: Avoid Public Transport: Using public transport
issues.explanation: Avoiding public transport is not well supported by the rest of the profile for childhood physical abuse by a caregiver. The listed triggers are arguments, crying, and unexpected touch, and the threat items center on interpersonal vigilance and positioning in rooms. Public transport avoidance suggests a different trigger/threat context and is hard to link coherently to the other selected items.

issues.item: Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building
issues.explanation: Avoiding being alone is not clearly connected to the rest of the profile. The threat items describe hypervigilance in shared spaces and interpersonal danger cues, while the triggers are interpersonal/emotional and tactile. Being alone as a primary avoidance target pulls toward a different clinical pattern unless there were accompanying abandonment or panic-related items, which are absent here.

Difficulty concentrating is a nonspecific PTSD symptom rather than a threat appraisal/perceived current danger item. Within this node, the other threat items specifically reflect situational safety behaviors and surveillance of the environment. This item does not fit the node's theme and weakens alignment with the formulation in which Threat is tightly linked to Maladaptive Strategies.

vignette:
Omar is a 19-year-old Middle Eastern American man who married young and now works as a junior environmental scientist, spending long days moving between a shared office, lab space, and field sites with older coworkers. In the first sessions he described a childhood shaped by physical abuse from a caregiver whose violence was often preceded by ordinary family conflict. He remembers arguments changing the air in the house before anything happened: voices sharpening behind a door, an adult face tightening, the sound of someone crying in another room. He learned to watch for those moments because they could be followed by being grabbed or hit without warning. What stayed with him most was not only the pain but the suddenness of it, the sense that once emotion showed on someone’s face, he had to be ready.

As he grew older, those early lessons did not fade. In the present, arguments are not just unpleasant to Omar; they feel like the beginning of danger. If two coworkers disagree in the office, or if he hears a couple bickering in a parking lot after work, his body reacts before he can talk himself down. Crying is especially difficult for him. When his wife tears up during a discussion, even if she is sad rather than angry, he feels a jolt of alarm and starts scanning her expression and posture, as if distress in another person could turn the room volatile at any second. Unexpected touch has a similar force. A colleague brushing past him in the lab or tapping his shoulder while he is focused can make him tense immediately, his mind jumping to the possibility that he has lost control of what is happening around him.

Because those moments set off such a strong sense of threat, Omar has come to organize himself around staying protected. He rarely sits casually anywhere. In meetings at the environmental office, he chooses a seat where his back is against the wall and he can see the door and everyone’s faces; if that seat is taken, he remains distracted and guarded through the whole discussion. He studies facial expressions and body language constantly, trying to tell who might escalate, who looks irritated, who seems too emotional. That vigilance shapes what he does next. He avoids conflict whenever he can, backing out of conversations that might involve disagreement, keeping his opinions brief, and sometimes agreeing with things he does not actually agree with just to keep tension from building. He also dislikes being by himself in a room or building and will linger near others at work rather than stay alone in a sampling room or return to the office after hours. At the same time, he often keeps distance from people generally, especially if he senses strong feeling in them, because being around them feels risky.

The vigilance itself has made him more reactive to the world around him. Because Omar is already reading every face and holding himself ready, arguments seem to flare brighter and faster for him than they do for other people. A small disagreement that others might dismiss catches his full attention; once he notices a hard look, a raised voice, or tears in someone’s eyes, he cannot stop tracking it. The more he watches for danger in people’s expressions and positions himself defensively, the easier it is for crying, confrontation, or a sudden touch to hit him like confirmation that something bad is about to happen. He described feeling as if his nervous system is “already halfway there,” so it takes very little to push him into alarm.

Over time, his ways of coping have narrowed his life and made those triggers feel even more loaded. By avoiding disagreement, he never gets the chance to find out that many arguments end without anyone being harmed; instead, conflict remains something he approaches as if it carries the same meaning it did in childhood. By steering away from people and dreading being alone, he spends much of the day preoccupied with where he can safely place himself rather than with the actual work in front of him. In the office this has become visible: he drifts to the edges of group discussions, chooses protected corners during team briefings, and times his movements so he is less likely to be startled by someone coming up beside him. His wife has begun to notice that even ordinary emotional conversations are hard to have with him. If she cries, he becomes watchful and withdrawn instead of comforting, which leaves both of them feeling alone.

What finally brought Omar to seek help was the accumulation of these moments at work and at home. He worries that he is living as if danger is always about to break out, and he is frightened by how quickly a raised voice, tears, or an unexpected touch can change the entire room for him. He says he wants to be able to sit through a meeting without planning escape routes and to be present with his wife when she is upset, but what he fears most is that if he lets his guard down even briefly, he will be caught unprepared again.
